newsitem.title: CANADA: WIC seen cutting jobs as TV battle looms.
newsitem.headline: WIC seen cutting jobs as TV battle looms.

text.p: The board of WIC Western International Communications Ltd is expected to approve layoffs and a restructuring charge on Friday in a bid to brace the Canadian broadcaster for new competition this year at its key television stations, analysts said.

A WIC spokesman confirmed the agenda for the Friday board meeting includes a restructuring plan for the company's television division. This would include some job cuts although no figures were available, he said.

Analysts said Thursday that WIC is under pressure to cut costs at its Albert and British Columbia television stations -- its strongest operations -- before new competitors go on air in both markets later this year.

WIC is due to announce late Friday results for its second fiscal quarter ended February 28. Analysts projected the company will include a restructuring provision of C$6 million to C$7 million to cover job cuts. The cuts are likely to be more extensive than steps taken by the company last year when about 67 jobs were eliminated.

In the second quarter a year ago WIC lost C$2.1 million after expenses of C$2.5 million to cover about 60 layoffs at two television stations. For 1996 as a whole, WIC earned C$8.3 million or C$0.33 a share including C$6 million in severance costs for two top executives and 67 other employees. For its first fiscal quarter to November, it earned C$8.3 million.

"Restructuring is a code word for layoffs. They are trying to reduce some costs on the labor side so they can focus more of their spending on programming" to ward off new competition, said one Toronto analyst who asked not to be identified.

Earlier this year, Craig Broadcast Systems Inc of Manitoba won licenses for new TV stations in Alberta and Baton Broadcasting Inc was awarded rights to a new station in Vancouver's coveted fast-growing market.
WIC is under pressure to protect its stations in the two markets which are its prize jewels. "They are likely to feel the impact of competition," said analyst Stephannie Larocque of Bunting Warburg.

Television accounts for about two-thirds of WIC's revenues. The broadcaster owns eight television stations, 12 radio stations, a share of Canada's CTV television network and has interests in pay television and satellite services.

WIC's strongest station is BCTV in Vancouver which boasts a commanding market share of about 46 percent. It also owns four television stations in Alberta including CICT in Calgary. Rival CanWest Global Communications Corp has long eyed the Alberta operations in hopes of gaining a foothold there.

The new competition comes on top of a a period of turmoil for WIC. Over the past year, it has faced pressure from shareholders who criticize its performance as lackluster, an aborted takeover bid from CanWest, a change in top management and a failed lawsuit that sought to wrest control of the company away from the founding Griffiths family.
